      Overlaps

      shared infrastructure between the corridors

      The proposal hypothesises that, despite polarising political rhetoric, the emerging routes overlap significantly in shared infrastructure and supply-chain hinterlands. This view measures the first part on the routed corridors: the same mapped rail line or sea leg used by two corridors, and the hubs and tracked nodes they share.

      Shared track between corridors (km) · diagonal: corridor length on the map

        Tracked ports and crossings on two or more corridors

          Projects

          World Bank · AIIB · ADB

          Projects in the eight corridor countries on transport, energy, digital or trade (China: western provinces only; urban projects left out), plus projects in Iraq, India, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Israel and Greece that name a Development Road or IMEC place. Each lender's full project list (World Bank API v3, AIIB project list, ADB's IATI files, EBRD project list) with the committed or approved amount; ADB and EBRD projects known only from contract awards are added with their contract value. Corridor tags need evidence in the project's own text: its name and the lender's own description.

          Contractors

          World Bank, ADB and EBRD awards

          Suppliers of World Bank-, ADB- and EBRD-financed contracts in corridor-layer projects, grouped by company: the seeds for the stakeholder map. The full list is out/stakeholder_seeds.csv.

              About

              method and limits

              Prototype tracker database for the UKRI project The Divergence-Convergence Nexus of Rival Connectivity Initiatives in Eurasia (CEPS, with METU Ankara and the Institute for China-Eurasia Studies, Yerevan). The project compares four routes: the BRI China–Central Asia–West Asia Economic Corridor (CCAWAEC), the EU Global Gateway flagship "Türkiye, South Caucasus, Central Asia connectivity", the Ankara-led Middle Corridor, and TRIPP. Its lens is political economy, the politics of infrastructure and industrial geography. It hypothesises that, despite polarising rhetoric, the routes overlap in shared infrastructure and supply-chain hinterlands, and asks which growth coalitions of officials, firms and lenders carry them at local, regional and transnational scale.

              Research questions. RQ1: how does the convergence of the Middle Corridor (EU and Türkiye versions), TRIPP and the CCAWAEC reconfigure regional power geometries? RQ2: how does the reopening of transport links between Azerbaijan and Armenia generate new frictions and alignments along the routes?

              The tracker serves the quantitative leg: performance indicators of the working routes, the overlaps between them, and the lenders and contractors behind them, as seeds for interviews in Ankara and Türkiye's border regions, Yerevan and Armenia's border areas, Kazakhstan and Brussels.

              Views

              • Map: the four corridors of the proposal, the North–South and northern routes via Russia for comparison, the Development Road and IMEC as linked initiatives, and the planned Black Sea power cable. Land legs follow the mapped rail network between the hubs in config/route_points.csv (see Route accuracy below). Shared stretches run side by side; dashed lines are sea legs; thin lines are branches.
              • Overlaps: shared track, hubs and nodes between the corridors, a first test of the overlap hypothesis.
              • Network (the growth coalitions in the data): the connections in the data. Corridors link to their ports and crossings; ports to countries; projects to their country, their lender, and a corridor where there is evidence (the project names the corridor, or names a place or section on its route, e.g. "Mangystau Oblast sections", "East–West Highway"; the panel shows the evidence); contractors to the projects they hold contracts on. Countries are anchored roughly at their geographic position, so the network reads west to east.
              • Ports, Trade, Projects, Contractors, Event log, Coverage: the tables behind it.

              Limits

              • Layer and corridor tags come from keywords and ADB's sector field, not hand coding.
              • PortWatch tonnes are far too low for Caspian ports, and Russian Caspian ports are largely dark (AIS off) in 2026.
              • Lenders loaded (checked for completeness on 6 Nov 2026): World Bank (projects API v3, incl. regional projects), AIIB (its full project list, with each project page's objective and description), ADB (its IATI files: loans and grants since about 2008, plus contract awards), EBRD (its project list with each project page's description, plus contracts signed since January 2026). The Development Road and IMEC countries (Iraq, India, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Israel, Greece) are read from the same sources, keeping only projects that name a place on those routes. IFC and MIGA, ADB technical assistance and proposed projects are not yet in. EIB loans and the CAREC projects database (IsDB, EFSD, EBRD financing) are read once their files are saved by hand into data/inbox/. Chinese lenders are not covered. Euro amounts are converted at the ECB rate of the signing month.
              • Event log: most entries were found by a search of news and official sites on 5 Nov 2026, the rest were entered by hand. Each links its source; the confidence column in data/manual/events.csv records which entries have been re-read at the source.

              Route accuracy

              Land legs follow the shortest path on the mapped rail network: Natural Earth 1:10m plus OpenStreetMap for the lines Natural Earth lacks (Khorgos–Altynkol, Zhezkazgan–Saksaulsk, Shalkar–Beineu, Akhalkalaki–Kars, Kazakhstan–Turkmenistan–Iran, Qazvin–Rasht, Bafq–Bandar Abbas, Marmaray, Angren–Pap and the Gulf lines). Line styles: solid = an existing line; dashed = a sea leg; wide dots = planned or under construction, drawn straight (China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan, Astara–Rasht, Kars–Iğdır–Nakhchivan, Horadiz–Meghri–Ordubad for TRIPP, Grand Faw–Basra and Mosul–Turkish border for the Development Road, Ghuwaifat–Haradh and Jordan–Haifa for IMEC, the Black Sea power cable). A faint solid line is an existing line the base map lacks, drawn straight (Astrakhan–Olya, the Riyadh link between the two Saudi networks). The routes are drawn by the researchers from the corridors' stated alignments, so where two corridors are drawn on the same line (Global Gateway on the Middle Corridor alignment) their overlap is partly by design. The report below lists each route's share on mapped rail. A mapped line is not necessarily in service: the TRIPP route follows the Soviet-era line along the Arax, closed since the early 1990s. Sea legs (Caspian ferries, Black Sea, Hormuz, Aegean) follow the busiest real shipping track between their ports in AIS ship-position data from January 2015 to February 2021, so they show the lanes before the war changed Black Sea routes; the Lake Van ferry has no AIS traffic and stays straight. The planned Black Sea power cable has no surveyed route yet and is drawn straight.

                Map sources

                • Natural Earth (public domain): country outlines, lakes, rail network (1:10m), rivers, cities.
                • OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL): rail lines Natural Earth lacks (Khorgos–Altynkol–Zhetygen, Zhezkazgan–Saksaulsk, Shalkar–Beineu, Baku–Tbilisi–Kars, Marmaray, Kazakhstan–Turkmenistan–Iran, Qazvin–Rasht, Bafq–Bandar Abbas); exact positions of Kuryk and Astara ports; trunk oil and gas pipelines (BTC, TANAP, TurkStream, Blue Stream, CPC, Kazakhstan–China, Beineu–Shymkent, Bukhara–Ural and others). The South Caucasus gas pipeline and the Central Asia–China gas pipeline are not mapped as routes in OpenStreetMap, and Beineu–Shymkent is only partly mapped.
                • TeleGeography Submarine Cable Map (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0): Black Sea and Caspian cables with year, length, owners and landing points.
                • World Bank / IMF Global Shipping Traffic Density, commercial vessels (CC BY 4.0; Cerdeiro, Komaromi, Liu and Saeed 2020, IMF World Seaborne Trade Monitoring System): hourly AIS positions, January 2015 to February 2021, on a 0.005° grid. Used to route the sea legs along the shipping lanes.
                • Not used: the NGA World Port Index (offline for maintenance when checked on 5 Nov 2026) and UN/LOCODE (blocks scripts).
